contributions.headingText: Nodular fasciitis is a self-limited mesenchymal neoplasm that usually occurs in subcutaneous tissue composed of plump fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells and usually harbours USP6 rearrangement.

Nodular fasciitis arises commonly in the subcutaneous tissues in conjunction with the fascial surface of the upper extremities, trunk, and head and neck in young adults, although it can occur at almost any anatomical location and in any age group {153036; 6462780; 1928550; 6279273}. Occasional cases arise in intramuscular and rarely intra-articular sites {16434899} or in the dermis {20716998; 8311183; 16640547}. Nodular fasciitis grows rapidly over a period of weeks or a few months and usually presents as a small, often tender nodule, rarely exceeding 50 mm {6462780; 1928550}. Uncommon subtypes of nodular fasciitis include intravascular fasciitis, arising in small and medium-sized blood vessels {8311183; 7246849; 34646860}, and cranial fasciitis, occurring commonly in the temporal and parietal deep layers of the scalp of young children (mostly infants), with common involvement of the underlying bone {7351023; 26703041}. The MRI features of nodular fasciitis are nonspecific, with a wide variety of imaging differential diagnoses {25467227; 11807586; 23624727}.

Nodular fasciitis is usually a cellular neoplasm composed of plump spindle to stellate cells with bland ovoid, vesicular nuclei with small nucleoli. Tumour cells are arranged in loose fascicles with a “tissue culture”–like growth pattern in fibromyxoid stroma. Storiform or whorled growth patterns may be observed in cellular areas. Stroma may be scant to abundant, with stromal matrix ranging from myxoid to densely collagenized, and often keloid-like in older lesions. Areas of cystic degeneration, mitoses, scattered lymphocytes, histiocytes, osteoclast-type giant cells, and extravasated erythrocytes are relatively common {6462780; 1928550; 6279273}. Osseous metaplasia may be seen in nodular and cranial fasciitis {6814399; 7351023}.

The main differential diagnoses of nodular fasciitis include pleomorphic, spindle cell, and myxoid sarcomas and desmoid fibromatosis. In contrast to nodular fasciitis, most high-grade sarcomas are composed of pleomorphic tumour cells containing irregular hyperchromatic nuclei with coarse chromatin and often prominent nucleoli, and atypical mitotic figures and necrosis are common. Synovial sarcomas may show bland cytopathological features {12722117}, but these neoplasms usually present as slowly growing, deep soft tissue masses and display characteristic ICC and molecular profiles {31161693} that distinguish them from nodular fasciitis. Smears of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans may mimic those of nodular fasciitis {12478683}, but the slow-growing and superficial dermal presentation, with bluish, red, or brown discolouration of the skin, is different from the subcutaneous location and rapid growth of nodular fasciitis.

Desmoid fibromatosis arises deeply, and it commonly infiltrates skeletal muscle. It produces less cellular smears and bland spindle cells separated by hyalinized collagenous and rarely myxoid stroma {17477374; 17260203}. Other soft tissue lesions sharing at least some cytopathological features with nodular fasciitis are granulomatous lesions, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour, schwannoma, and neurofibroma. All of these lesions show clinical features and ICC profiles distinct from those of nodular fasciitis. Smears of nodular fasciitis in the head and neck region can be confused with pleomorphic adenoma due to the myxoid stroma and spindle myoepithelial cells, but features such as a predominance of spindle cells with cytoplasmic processes, prominent nucleoli, and occasional mitoses favour a diagnosis of nodular fasciitis over pleomorphic adenoma {25472697; 30311731; 23749727; 16078254}.

Proliferative fasciitis and proliferative myositis are pseudosarcomatous lesions closely related to, but much less common than, nodular fasciitis. Both occur predominantly in middle-aged or older adults {1058047; 6073898; 14408614}, with a rare subtype of proliferative fasciitis described in children {1566969}. The clinical course of these lesions mimics that of nodular fasciitis; they grow rapidly, rarely exceeding 50 mm, and are often tender or painful. Proliferative fasciitis most commonly develops in the subcutaneous tissue of the upper extremities, followed by the lower extremities and trunk, whereas proliferative myositis arises intramuscularly, most commonly in the trunk, followed by the shoulder girdles, upper arms, and less often thighs. Both proliferative fasciitis and proliferative myositis share many FNAB features with nodular fasciitis, such as spindle cells with cytoplasmic processes and round or oval nuclei in addition to plump polygonal, epithelioid cells and a variable number of ganglion-like cells with prominent nucleoli {1586481; 8785374; 20890998; 23326034}. The myxoid background matrix is less prominent and the ganglion-like cells are usually numerous and often exhibit large nucleoli in proliferative fasciitis. In proliferative myositis, smears contain multinucleated regenerating muscle fibres in addition to the fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells {12462081}. Mitotic figures can be found in both lesions. The ICC profile is similar to that of nodular fasciitis {2058761; 1586481; 8785374}, but unlike in nodular fasciitis, neither a recurrent genomic abnormality nor translocation has been found in these lesions.

Nodular fasciitis expresses SMA, calponin, and CD10. Desmin, h-caldesmon, S100, and CD34 are negative. CD68 is positive in intralesional osteoclast-like multinucleated cells {1928550; 25890487}. β-catenin expression can be positive in some cranial fasciitis cases {18587328}. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans demonstrates positivity for CD34.

The majority of nodular fasciitis cases are characterized by recurrent translocations involving USP6, and the MYH9::USP6 fusion product is the most common, found in two thirds of cases {21826056; 28752842}. Other USP6 gene fusion partners have also been described {28752842}. USP6 rearrangements are not specific to nodular fasciitis; they can also be found in other benign soft tissue and bone tumours, such as myositis ossificans and aneurysmal bone cyst {27271298; 29661729; 23769422}. USP6 rearrangements can be identified by FISH, PCR, or NGS {28752842; 27271298; 34381187}. The percentage of break-apart FISH signals decreases during ageing of nodular fasciitis, which can be a potential source of false negative results in older lesions {34381187}.
